solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Crew member’s company detains sailor in Boar’s Head (5,3)

indicatorNotes.detains: to detain is to hold someone in custody, so the company holds the other letters inside it
indicatorNotes.Head: the head of anything is its top, so the head of Boar is its first letter

blocks.note: Coy. is the military abbreviation for company

annotation.surface: A sailor is kept drinking at the Boar’s Head, a pub, by his shipmates.
annotation.walkthrough: Coy. for company is an army abbreviation rarely seen outside military lists, so the usual CO misleads here. The Boar’s Head reads as a pub name.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain description: a cabin boy is the youngest hand on a ship, waiting on officers, so a member of its crew.

entries.clue: Commander, completely upset, initially resisted arrest (6)

indicatorNotes.upset: to upset something is to knock it over, and in a down clue that turns the word upside down
indicatorNotes.initially: initially means at the start, so take the first letter of resisted

annotation.surface: An angry commander is resisting arrest.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'arrest' part of the story, but it is the definition, sitting at the far end.
annotation.definitionFit: Informal police slang: to grab a suspect by the collar is to arrest them, so the noun became the verb.

entries.clue: Singer is mafia grass according to Spooner (3,6)

indicatorNotes.according to Spooner: the Reverend Spooner was famous for swapping the first sounds of words, so do what he would do

blocks.note: mob = mafia; takes the B from the next word
barley is a cereal grass; takes the M from the first word

annotation.surface: A singer is revealed as a police informer against the mafia.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Grass' reads as British slang for an informer, but it is the cereal plant barley.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Jamaican reggae star is one singer among many.

entries.clue: Dancer’s series returning — watch on 5 (7)

indicatorNotes.returning: to return is to go back the way you came, so the series runs backwards
indicatorNotes.on: in a down clue, one thing on another sits above it, so the watch goes on top of the 5

annotation.surface: A dancer’s television series comes back, to be watched on channel 5.
annotation.walkthrough: '5' looks like a TV channel, but it is just the Roman numeral.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Rudolf Nureyev was the most famous ballet dancer of his era.

entries.clue: Nothing soppy about beginning to like little bird (5)

indicatorNotes.about: about means around, so the soppy word goes around the letter
indicatorNotes.beginning to: the beginning of a word is its first letter, so take the L of like

annotation.surface: Someone insists there is nothing soppy about starting to like little birds.
annotation.walkthrough: Wet, in British speech, means weak and soppy as well as damp.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the -let ending means small, so a young owl is literally a little bird.

entries.clue: Infatuation with books about language (6)

indicatorNotes.about: to turn about is to face the other way, so the books are reversed

blocks.note: pash = a schoolgirl crush, British slang

annotation.surface: Someone has a crush on books about language.
annotation.walkthrough: A pash is dated British slang for a crush.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: this is the tongue of the Pashtun people of Afghanistan and Pakistan, one language among many.

entries.clue: Beer guzzling job for true believer (7)

indicatorNotes.guzzling: to guzzle is to swallow greedily, so the beer swallows the job whole

annotation.surface: Drinking beer is a job for a real enthusiast.
annotation.walkthrough: Beyond the twelve disciples, the word is used of any passionate advocate of a cause.
annotation.definitionFit: An extended sense: the first followers sent out by Jesus give a name to any fervent believer or champion.

entries.clue: Run in stockings for Jade, perhaps (5)

indicatorNotes.in: one thing in another is inside it, so the run sits within the stockings

blocks.note: R = run, as in cricket scores

annotation.surface: A woman called Jade has a ladder in her stockings.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Run' is a ladder in tights, and Jade looks like a woman’s name; a jade is an old, worn-out nag.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example, flagged by 'perhaps': a jade is a tired or worthless specimen of the animal.

entries.clue: Extrovert in latter stages of incumbency? (8)

blocks.note: an extrovert is sociable and friendly
said of an office-holder about to leave the post

annotation.surface: A sociable office-holder nears the end of their term.
annotation.walkthrough: Both senses are adjectives; the second is the one used of a president or chairman about to step down.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses of one word: friendly and sociable, and departing from office, as in the outgoing government.

entries.clue: Succeed, for example, after experiencing setback? Thanks, boss (3,5)

indicatorNotes.after experiencing setback: a setback sets something back, so the example abbreviation is turned round

annotation.surface: Someone thanks their boss for helping them succeed after a setback.
annotation.walkthrough: Ta is everyday British for thank you.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: to move in front of rivals in life or a career is to succeed.

entries.clue: After abundant protest, whip accepts Republican Party member (7,8)

indicatorNotes.accepts: to accept something is to take it in, so the whip takes the Republican inside
indicatorNotes.After: after means following, so the whip comes after abundant protest

blocks.note: a liberal helping = an abundant one

annotation.surface: After a big protest, a party whip lets a Republican join.
annotation.walkthrough: Whip and party read as parliamentary jargon; the whip is a lash. The Liberal Democrats are a British political party.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a Lib Dem belongs to one of Britain’s main political parties.

entries.clue: Register reportedly concludes article by American pundit (7)

indicatorNotes.reportedly: what is reported is heard rather than read, so the register is taken by sound
indicatorNotes.concludes: to conclude is to come at the end, so the register goes last
indicatorNotes.by: by means beside, so the American sits next to the article

annotation.surface: A register records that an article was concluded by an American commentator.
annotation.walkthrough: The register comes first in the clue but last in the answer, because it concludes the rest.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a pundit is an expert who studies events and comments on them, the analyst’s job.

entries.clue: Firm following free trade style (3,4)

indicatorNotes.following: following means coming after, so the firm goes after the rearranged letters
indicatorNotes.free: freed letters are no longer tied to their order, so trade is rearranged

annotation.surface: A company adopts a free-trade way of doing business.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Free trade' looks like economics; 'free' is only there to rearrange the second word.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the geometric design look of the 1920s and 30s is one artistic style.

entries.clue: Bone’s depleted cell area left in clamp (8)

indicatorNotes.depleted: something depleted has been emptied, so cell loses its middle and keeps its outside
indicatorNotes.in: one thing in another is inside it, so left goes within the clamp

blocks.note: CELL emptied of its middle letters
a vice is a clamping tool

annotation.surface: A bone lies in a shrunken prison cell, held in a clamp.
annotation.walkthrough: Vice is the British spelling of the clamp Americans call a vise.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the collarbone is one bone of the skeleton.

entries.clue: Stupid advice to overworked setter? (8)

blocks.note: an overworked setter should write fewer clues; split the answer 4 + 4

annotation.surface: Someone gives a stupid piece of advice to a tired crossword setter.
annotation.walkthrough: The second half is cryptic: split the answer as CLUE LESS, an instruction to a setter with too many clues to write.
annotation.definitionFit: Two readings: an informal synonym for stupid, and literally 'write fewer clues', the advice.

entries.clue: The Spanish film’s last caption’s mischievous (5)

blocks.note: FIN, 'the end', closes many old films

annotation.surface: A Spanish film ends with a playful caption.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Last' tempts you to take a final letter, but the whole French word for 'end' is the film's last caption.
annotation.definitionFit: An extended sense: like an elf, so impish and playfully mischievous.

entries.clue: Onset of frost threatened to overwhelm British garden feature (9)

indicatorNotes.Onset of: the onset of something is its start, so take the first letter of frost
indicatorNotes.to overwhelm: to overwhelm is to engulf, so the threatening word swamps the B and holds it inside

blocks.note: to lower (rhymes with flower) = to scowl, look threatening

annotation.surface: The first frost threatens to ruin a British garden.
annotation.walkthrough: Lower here is the verb pronounced like 'flower', meaning to frown or look menacing, as a dark sky does.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a planted plot is one feature a garden may have.

entries.clue: Spoiled international politician given publicity (8)

annotation.surface: A spoilt international politician gets media attention.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Spoiled' reads as pampered but means damaged.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the sense of damaged: something spoiled has been weakened or harmed.

entries.clue: Perhaps millions live on for ever (5)

indicatorNotes.on: in an across clue, one thing on another is added after it, so live follows for ever

annotation.surface: Perhaps millions of people will live for ever.
annotation.walkthrough: Aye for always is poetic and Scottish, and may be spelt with or without the E.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both are adverbs of possibility that swap freely in 'X it will rain'.

entries.clue: Composed more war music that drives people crazy (7)

indicatorNotes.Composed: to compose is to put together, so the letters are assembled anew

annotation.surface: A composer writes more war music, a tune that maddens listeners.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Composed' fits the music surface perfectly, which hides its job of rearranging the letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: a catchy tune stuck in the head, playing over and over until it maddens you.

entries.clue: Fewer than 500 try backing unlikely winner (8)

indicatorNotes.backing: backing is moving backwards, so the try is read in reverse

annotation.surface: Fewer than 500 people bet on the outsider.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Backing' reads as betting, which suits an outsider; it means reverse.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: the competitor expected to lose would be an unlikely one to win.

entries.clue: Observe others keeping quiet on city (7)

indicatorNotes.keeping: to keep something is to hold it, so the others hold the rest inside
indicatorNotes.on: in a down clue, one thing on another sits above it, so quiet goes on top of city

blocks.note: EC = the City of London postcode

annotation.surface: Watch the others staying quiet about the city.
annotation.walkthrough: The City, the financial district of London, has the postcode EC. 'Observe' is not watching but obeying.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the sense of abiding by: to observe a law or custom is to honour it.

entries.clue: Caught somebody without European pass (6)

indicatorNotes.without: without means lacking, so somebody goes without its European letter

annotation.surface: Someone was caught without a valid European travel pass.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pass' looks like a document, but it is a way through mountains.
annotation.definitionFit: A loose synonym: a pass is a route through mountains, and a deep gorge can serve as one.

entries.clue: Trim line on archbishop’s cloak and dress (7)

indicatorNotes.on: in an across clue, one thing on another is added after it, so trim and line follow
indicatorNotes.cloak: a cloak wraps around the outside, so the cloak of archbishop is its first and last letters

annotation.surface: A tailor trims the edging on an archbishop’s cloak and robes.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Archbishop’s cloak' reads as a vestment; it means only the letters that wrap the word.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both nouns mean clothing, as in 'evening dress'.

entries.clue: Writing introduction to perennial beauty (5)

indicatorNotes.introduction to: an introduction comes first, so take the first letter of perennial

blocks.note: a rose, as a beauty among flowers

annotation.surface: An essay introduces a beautiful perennial plant.
annotation.walkthrough: Perennial and beauty both sound like gardening, which fits the flower neatly.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: ordinary, non-verse language is one kind of writing.

entries.clue: Part of mosaic seen in square’s setting from the east (7)

indicatorNotes.seen in: something seen in a place is visible inside it, so the letters sit within the words
indicatorNotes.from the east: in an across clue, east is the right-hand end, so read from right to left

annotation.surface: A mosaic tile appears in a square’s pattern, viewed from the east side.
annotation.walkthrough: Mosaic, square and setting all belong together, which helps hide the backwards letters across the apostrophe.
annotation.definitionFit: A precise term: the small cube of stone or glass set into a mosaic, one part of the whole.

entries.clue: Bizet ultimately snubbed award for opera (5)

indicatorNotes.ultimately: ultimately means in the end, so take the last letter of Bizet
indicatorNotes.snubbed: a snub nose is cut short, so the award loses its end

blocks.note: the Oscar film award, minus its last letter

annotation.surface: Bizet was finally passed over for an opera prize.
annotation.walkthrough: Bizet wrote Carmen, so the surface points to the wrong composer; 'snubbed' cuts the end off, like a snub nose.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Puccini’s tragedy is one opera among many.

entries.clue: Absolutism rose disastrously before conclusion of bloody disorder (7,8)

indicatorNotes.disastrously: a disaster leaves things in chaos, so the letters are thrown into a new order
indicatorNotes.before: before means in front of, so the fodder comes ahead of the Y
indicatorNotes.conclusion of: the conclusion is the end, so take the last letter of bloody

annotation.surface: Absolute rule rose disastrously before ending in bloody disorder.
annotation.walkthrough: The Y joins the anagram fodder. The answer is also an old British legal term for a violent gathering.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a violent, unruly gathering is one form of public disorder.

entries.clue: Simply gorgeous model my dear (6)

indicatorNotes.model: to model clay is to shape it, so the letters are shaped into a new form

annotation.surface: Someone gushes to a model, calling her simply gorgeous.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Model' reads as a person being flattered; it is the verb, shaping the last two words.
annotation.definitionFit: An informal synonym: something so lovely it seems out of a dream is simply gorgeous.

entries.clue: Love in staff party ending in conviction for old beast (8)

indicatorNotes.in: one thing in another is inside it, so love sits within staff party
indicatorNotes.ending in: the ending of a word is its last letter, so take the N of conviction

blocks.note: a mast is a pole, a staff

annotation.surface: An office romance at the staff party ends in a conviction for an old brute.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Staff party' looks like one office event, but staff is a pole and the love goes between the two words.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the extinct elephant-like animal is one ancient beast.
